Part 1: The Frame

The frame carries everything. It is welded from square tube, and building it teaches most of Part Design.

Part 1: The Frame01 / 11

Reading the source

What the tutorial gives us

What it says

  • “A centre rectangle, 82 inches and a height of 22 inches”
  • “Square tube, size 0.1875”
  • “One hole here and another hole here”
  • “The hole size is 3 inches”
  • “The distance is 9.5 inches, we need 9 patterns”

What we make of it

  • Each station is a pair of holes, 3 inches apart. The 3 inches is the spacing, not a diameter.
  • The tyne, later in the same video, gets two bolts 3 inches apart. They match, so the machine bolts together.
  • 0.1875 is the wall thickness, not the tube size. We use 2 × 2 inch tube, which is normal for a light cultivator.

The brackets at each end are the tractor's lower link points. A pair 15 inches out from the centre gives 30 inches between them, which is the standard spacing.

Part 1: The Frame02 / 11

Parameters

Put the numbers in a spreadsheet first

Before you draw a line, write the dimensions into a spreadsheet and give each one a name.

  1. Switch to the Spreadsheet workbench and create a sheet
  2. Type the name, the value with its unit, and what it means82 in
  3. Click the value cell and press Alias, then type the name
  4. Later, in any dimension box, click the small blue circle and type the nameParams.FrameLength

Do this first and it is painless. Retro-fitting it to a finished part is a chore.

Part 1: The Frame03 / 11

Sketch and pad

The outline: two rectangles

Seen from above, a rectangular tube frame is just two rectangles, one inside the other.

  1. Sketch on the XY plane
  2. Centred rectangle, 82 × 22 — the outside
  3. Second centred rectangle, 78 × 18 — the inside
  4. Pad the ring 2 inches= tube size

SolidWorks would use the Weldments tool here. FreeCAD has no equivalent, and for a four-sided frame it does not need one.

Part 1: The Frame04 / 11

A cut that starts inside the metal

Making the tube hollow

Right now the frame is solid bar and weighs 227 pounds. Real tube is hollow.

  1. New sketch on the XY plane
  2. Set its attachment offset so it floats just under the top wallz = 1.8125 in
  3. Draw two more rectangles: the inside of the tube walls
  4. Pocket down through the middle1.625 in

A pocket cuts from its sketch plane, downwards. If you sketch on the top face, the pocket eats the top wall. Start it just below the wall instead and you get a proper hollow tube.

Part 1: The Frame05 / 11

Symmetry doing the work

One tyne station

A tyne station is two bolts, 3 inches apart. Both bars need the same stations.

  1. Sketch on the XY plane, offset up to the top facez = 2 in
  2. First circle, half an inch across, positioned from the origin
  3. Second circle 3 inches along, and Equal to the first3 in
  4. Two more circles, made Symmetric about the X axis, for the rear bar
  5. Pocket, through all

All four holes go in one sketch. Deck 11 explains why — it saves a real headache further on.

Part 1: The Frame06 / 11

Linear pattern

Nine stations from one

One station becomes nine, and both the count and the spacing come from the spreadsheet.

  1. Select the pocket in the tree
  2. Part Design › LinearPattern
  3. Direction: the body's X axis
  4. Mode Extent, length 76 inches8 &times; 9.5
  5. Occurrences: 9including the original

Extent spreads the copies across a total length. Spacing puts a fixed gap between them. Use Extent here, so changing the count keeps the holes on the frame.

Part 1: The Frame07 / 11

Sketching away from the plane

The hitch brackets

Each lower link needs a fork: two plates with a gap between them for the tractor's ball end.

  1. Sketch on the YZ plane
  2. Offset it out to where the first plate face goes15.75 in
  3. Draw the plate outline: 5 inches long, 3 inches tall
  4. Pad it0.4 in
  5. Repeat on the other side of the gap, with Reversed ticked

We model the 1.5 inch gap directly, because that is the dimension that has to fit the tractor.

Part 1: The Frame08 / 11

Mirrored

Pin hole, then mirror

Build one side properly, then mirror it. Half the work, and the two sides can never drift apart.

  1. Sketch a 1 inch circle on the YZ plane, halfway between the plates15 in
  2. Pocket, through all, with Symmetric to plane ticked
  3. Select both pads and the pocket
  4. Part Design › Mirrored, about the YZ plane

Symmetric plus Through all cuts both ways at once, so one feature drills both plates.

Part 1: The Frame09 / 11

When FreeCAD says no

A fillet that cannot exist

The tutorial asks for a rounded end on the bracket. Our first attempt failed, and it is worth understanding why.

  • We asked for a 0.63 inch round on the two edges of the bracket nose.
  • The nose is only 0.4 inches wide — the plate thickness. There is not enough metal, so FreeCAD refused.
  • The fix is to round the corners of the outline instead, where the plate is 3 inches tall.

SolidWorks has a full-round fillet that replaces a face with a half-round. FreeCAD does not. Rounding both corners gets you the same look.

  • No feature is marked failed.
